title: Roots of Democracy — Match the Thinker
hint: Each statement reflects a single core idea — consent, the general will, separation of powers, or harm to others. Two of the statements describe positions that don't fit democratic theory.
distractors: Government should be in the hands of those most fit to rule — wise philosopher-kings trained for the task — not the unwise multitude.
True political wisdom comes from a society's inherited traditions and institutions, not from abstract theories of natural rights or popular sovereignty.

feedback.correct: Excellent! You've matched each thinker with their key contribution to democratic theory. Locke gives us consent and natural rights; Rousseau, the general will; Montesquieu, the separation of powers; Mill, the protection of individual liberty from the tyranny of the majority.
feedback.incorrect: Review the matches. Locke (consent + natural rights), Rousseau (general will + popular sovereignty), Montesquieu (separation of powers), and Mill (liberty + the harm principle) each named a distinct mechanism that modern democracies still rest on. The two unmatched statements describe Plato's philosopher-kings (anti-democratic) and Burke's traditionalist conservatism (a critique of abstract democratic theory) — both important in political thought, but outside the canonical roots of democracy.

pairs.match: Government's authority comes from the consent of the governed; people retain natural rights to life, liberty, and property that no ruler can rightfully take away.
Legitimate political authority arises from the 'general will' of the people. True freedom is found in obeying laws we have collectively made for ourselves.
Liberty is preserved by separating the powers of government — legislative, executive, and judicial — so that no one body holds absolute power.
Individual liberty must be protected even from the will of the majority. The only justification for limiting another's freedom is to prevent harm to others.
